Yes, the story has an appropriate balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

Because the narrative spans an entire academic year (from October to spring) and explores Mara's evolving dynamics with four different characters, the writer effectively uses summary and exposition to compress time, establish character backgrounds, and reflect on Mara's internal growth (e.g., summarizing how her closeness with Carl grew over weeks, or how she changed by spring). At the same time, the story dramatizes the pivotal turning points in real-time scenes with sharp dialogue and specific actions—such as confronting Carl in the library about his essay, the kiss with Martin at the café, the falling-out and eventual reconciliation with Lizzy, and looking at photographs with Johan. This interplay allows the story to cover a wide span of time and emotional development at a steady pace without feeling either rushed or bogged down.
